lesson.title: Shantytowns of Shame: Hoovervilles and the Face of the Depression
lesson.summary: As homelessness spread and the federal government seemed unable to help, unemployed Americans built makeshift shantytowns nicknamed Hoovervilles, a bitter and highly visible rebuke of President Hoover's response to the crisis.
lesson.body:
As unemployment soared and evictions and foreclosures mounted in the wake of the bank failures and economic collapse described in earlier chapters, growing numbers of Americans found themselves without homes. Many built makeshift shelters out of scrap wood, cardboard, tin, and tar paper on vacant lots, in city parks, and along riverbanks. These shantytowns sprang up in cities large and small across the country.

The nickname that stuck to them, Hooverville, was a pointed political jab, often credited to Charles Michelson, the publicity director for the Democratic National Committee, who worked to pin blame for the Depression's suffering squarely on President Hoover. The name fit into a wider pattern of grim, sarcastic humor built around the president's name: newspapers used for warmth were called Hoover blankets, empty pockets turned inside out were Hoover flags, and broken-down automobiles pulled by mules for lack of gasoline money were Hoover wagons.

Hoovervilles appeared in a great many places. A well-documented example stood in New York City's Central Park, and large encampments also formed in Seattle along the tideflats and in St. Louis along the Mississippi riverfront, among many other cities. Their size and how long they persisted varied considerably from place to place, and some lasted for years, well into the early New Deal era.

More than any statistic, Hoovervilles made the human cost of the Depression impossible to ignore. They turned Hoover's name into a shorthand for government indifference to suffering in the public memory of the era, and they fed the growing anger and desperation that would soon erupt in an even more dramatic confrontation between struggling Americans and the federal government: the Bonus Army march on Washington.
